nameStory: The 'mealy-rimmed' part of this lichen's name comes from its distinctive powdery white edges that look like they've been dusted with flour or cornmeal. The 'shingle' refers to how its leaf-like lobes overlap each other like roof shingles, creating a layered, textured appearance on tree bark.
description: Mealy-rimmed Shingle Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms small to medium-sized patches on tree bark in New England's forests. Its blue-gray to brownish lobes overlap like tiny shingles, each rimmed with a characteristic white, powdery margin that gives it its distinctive appearance. Individual patches typically grow 2-4 inches across, though older specimens can spread wider over many years of slow growth.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: White, powdery rim around each lobe that feels slightly gritty when rubbed gently - this mealy edge is the key identifying feature that sets it apart from other shingle lichens

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Leafy lobes that overlap each other like roof shingles, forming rosette-like patches that lie fairly flat against the bark

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Blue-gray to brownish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant blue-green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like beech and maple

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically 2-4 inches across, with lobes about 1/4 to 1/2 inch wide

habitat: This uncommon lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees in New England's mature forests, showing a strong preference for smooth-barked trees like American beech, sugar maple, and yellow birch. It tends to favor humid, sheltered locations in rich woodlands at various elevations, often in areas with consistent moisture and filtered light.

seasonality.spring: Easy to spot when spring rains bring out its blue-green colors, making the white mealy rim particularly striking against the darker, moistened lobes.
seasonality.summer: May appear more muted and gray during dry spells, but the characteristic white rim remains visible and diagnostic even when the lichen looks dormant.
seasonality.fall: Often looks refreshed after autumn rains, with colors becoming more vibrant as deciduous host trees drop their leaves and allow more moisture to reach the bark.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible and identifiable year-round, though colors may be more subdued; the mealy rim stays prominent even under snow and ice.

funFact: Despite being called 'mealy-rimmed,' that white powder isn't actually meal at all - it's made up of tiny fungal structures called soredia that can break off and start new lichen colonies elsewhere, essentially making each rim a launch pad for baby lichens!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other shingle lichens, but the distinctive white, powdery rim makes identification straightforward - if you see that mealy edge, you've found your lichen! Other shingle lichens may have similar growth forms but lack this telltale floury border.
compareHints: While it's the only Pannaria species commonly found in New England, it can be distinguished from similar-looking foliose lichens in other families by its distinctive mealy white rim and preference for deciduous tree bark. Most other overlapping, shingle-like lichens either lack the powdery edge entirely or have different reproductive structures like cup-shaped fruiting bodies instead of the scattered soredia.
